scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

This geographic narrative describes named archaeological sites, historical communities and later institutions within the area of Guyana. The approximate 2900 BCE opening is a selected archaeological window, not first settlement or state formation. The 1627 phase uses Fort Nassau as a reference point rather than the beginning of all European contact. Indigenous communities continue. No unverified successor links are added.

Plew and Daggers’ Siriki report was read in its original Antiquity text and Cambridge mirror. The basal sample is 4140 plus or minus 30 radiocarbon years BP, calibrated to 4820 to 4750 and 4730 to 4530 cal BP, broadly the third millennium BCE. Uncalibrated BP is not mechanically converted into a calendar date. A later sample suggests reuse; the card does not imply all deposits, foods or tools date to one event. The apparent centimetre depth typo for the later sample is not repeated.

Quartz cores suggest on-site reduction and worked flakes show tool production or use; the report explicitly leaves the precise food-processing task unresolved. Archaeological Alaka phase terminology is not converted into an ethnic identity. Fragmentary human remains are not used to invent family relationships, care practices or heights.

The National Trust architectural guide was read through the PDF text, especially printed pages 18, 19, 21, 27 and 28. Cottages, yard facilities, decorative roofing and window construction are architectural types and purposes, not a census of Guyanese houses. Ice cooling is described by the guide and not assumed affordable to everyone. Bird-deterring ironwork is not proof that collected rainwater was safe. No present-day construction or sanitation directions are offered.

The guide’s assertion that Georgetown gained city status in 1912, its sweeping account of seasonal Indigenous coastal occupation, and unsupported claims of European priority in permanent settlement are excluded. The source’s proposed World Heritage nomination is not presented as an inscription. Historical household water volumes and units are not needed and are omitted.

Camp Street Koker’s nineteenth-century origin and circa 1938 rehabilitation remain approximate. The entry describes an irrigation function and is not used to assert a particular tidal operating sequence or that all drainage structures worked identically.

Victoria’s 1839 collective purchase and 1841 title are separate stages. The National Trust’s story of transporting buried savings in a wheelbarrow, a first-village superlative and currency conversion are not repeated. Freed people are identified as formerly enslaved, not as slaves after emancipation. The archive document is described through the heritage account; a scan of the title has not been personally inspected.

The library’s 1909 opening, 1935 museum accommodation and 1951 museum departure are separate events. The paragraph is dated 1951 to prevent the later facts appearing contemporary with 1909. The building’s public name does not prove equal access for all people in colonial society.

The DPI 2019 report documents a specific demonstration with older Indigenous craftspeople and student participation. Its sweeping dying-culture description and political praise are not adopted. No promised future programme is assumed to have occurred, and no child’s name is reproduced.

David Aickin’s 2001 doctoral thesis was downloaded and relevant pages read, including hospital facilities, maternal mortality, midwifery and dairy regulation. The maternity ward’s post-1894 relocation and the 1908 children’s ward description are dated observations. Facilities alone do not demonstrate safety or clinical effectiveness. Colonial physicians’ racist and class-based judgments of mothers and local midwives are not adopted, and no historical drug regimen is provided as advice.

The dairy regulations are dated by the cited September 1912 publication, while protests and negotiations discussed in the following pages occurred in January 1913. The paragraph is a history of regulation, not a statement of complete compliance or a technical specification. It does not blame poor households for structural sanitation problems.

The joint archival nomination’s Guyana range is 1838 to 1917. Its claims that the records are the only genealogical source and that all four nominating states are islands are rejected. No personal record is accessed or reproduced, and the text does not claim all documents survive or are digitised. SAADA supplies the separate migration chronology; no full oral-history interview or book is claimed as read.

Phagwah’s 2025 description is a dated account of practices, not a current event listing or a claim that everyone participates. Hindu narrative and religious meaning are distinguished from a physical historical claim. The official report’s broad assertions that celebrations eliminate division are not repeated. Humour concerns clothing colours, not religious belief.

The colonial history separates British control in 1803 from formal cession in 1814 and union as British Guiana in 1831. The U.S. diplomatic guide’s summary incorrectly associates cession with the Congress of Vienna; it is used only for independence in 1966. Huygens ING’s supported 1814 treaty chronology is used instead. Its wider judgments of colonial development and Indigenous relations are not adopted.

The National Trust emancipation account is used only for the local 1834 and 1838 distinction. Its inaccurate or conflicting monument dedication details, simplified causal explanation for ending apprenticeship and exact imperial legislative dates are omitted. Parliament’s summary of Court of Policy membership is not assumed unchanged throughout 1831 to 1928.

The 1953 constitution and its suspension, independence in 1966, republican status in 1970 and executive presidency in 1980 are separate transitions. Later governments are not collapsed into one ruler, and no current officeholder or legal advice is given. The Huygens source is also used by the Suriname card; their combined prose and source labels remain within the source summary budget.

Several National Trust and old Parliament pages redirect or fail on direct opening; their relevant complete indexed text was read. The architecture PDF and archival nomination were read through the web reader, and the UCL thesis locally. Access limits do not imply independent endorsement of all claims on those pages.
The new narrative is author-checked and awaits independent historical review.

identityEvidence.assessment: The Guyana record depicts the country’s area and starts during British colonial government. Its 1914 opening is map coverage, not independence. The separately imported british-guiana and guiana outlines cover different extents, including Suriname, and are not attached. Geometry is unchanged; this narrative does not adjudicate territorial disputes or certify borders.
